newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Old tramp says world bums' summit too New Age.
newsitem.headline: Old tramp says world bums' summit too New Age.

text.p: International tramps opened their first world conference at an Argentine seaside resort on Tuesday but a veteran hobo said modern vagabonds were often merely trendy vegetarians.
Organisers said some 300 delegates from as far afield as Greece, Canada and Colombia might turn up in Mar del Plata.
"Many people suffer from stress, which is one of the illnesses that work gives you," Pedro Ribeiro, the 57-year-old founder of the Free Tramps Movement, told Reuters.

"We thought presidents have many summits, but travelers, the anonymous people, also need to talk among themselves of their problems, how to go about being a wanderer," said Ribeiro, who summoned the world's free-spirited wanderers to sow revolt against the slavery of work.

Mario Alonso, a bearded potter in a greasy cap, came to Mar del Plata from his adobe home near El Bolson, an idyllic refuge for ecologists and ageing hippies among the lakes and mountains of Argentina's far southern region of Patagonia.

A vegetarian who plans to give a talk on bartering goods and thus avoiding money, Alonso proudly demonstrated his tramp's dining kit made up of seven different-sized tin cans for use as a stove, tea pot, plates and cups.
The well-informed modern tramp knows how to eat cheaply and well, he said. "For food, well I don't eat meat. We can just go out into the country and there is food. Nature provides food for you."
But 82-year old Hector Woollands, who roamed Argentina penniless in the 1930s and now lives humbly in Mar del Plata, has his doubts about the New Age sheen of today's tramps.

"These ones today, they're phony tramps. They're idealists but not tramps," he told reporters. "The old ones liked tobacco, some also liked to drink a bit. They're weren't after a healthy life and they weren't fussy about what they ate to look after their health."

But Ribeira sees the modern tramp as a philosopher, a lover of liberty and the sworn foe of materialism. "The tramp shows total solidarity, shares his food, his knowledge, education and goods and donates his blood and organs selflessly," he said.

"Tramps know there are poor people, people so poor that they only have work," he added, quoting from a "tramps' manifesto" prepared by the movement. But he admits many of those turning up are less drifters than dreamers, recreational wanderers who want to "recapture the spirit of the tramp."
He himself is a jazz musician with a comfortable Mar del Plata home. But he also has a walk to Rio de Janeiro -- more than 1,500 miles (2,400 km) north -- to his credit.
The week of activities includes a non-competitive hike, in which participants struggle to walk no faster than anyone else, and is programmed to culminate in a "big feed."
Those addicted to work are being admitted as observers.
